slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 18: Building Data Pipelines with Ranges and Views. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

A range provides a begin/end traversal interface, potentially with different iterator and sentinel types. Range-based algorithms can accept that range directly, reducing repeated endpoint plumbing and enabling constrained interfaces. The range is an access abstraction, not necessarily an owner. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 18, treat Separate the recipe from the result as a design decision with costs and evidence. The worked sequence creates a view that selects even numbers and squares them. It then iterates to build an owning vector. The view is a recipe over the current source; the vector is a materialized result. Sorting the result changes only that owned result, not the original source or the mathematical definition of the recipe. The second traversal after a source change deliberately uses a newly constructed filtering pipeline. This avoids teaching that a previously traversed view must forget all cached state when the source changes. The program demonstrates a controlled lifecycle: establish source state, construct a view, consume it within that state, end its use, change the source, and construct a fresh view. slides.title: Failure clinic — A returned pipeline that borrows a dead vector
keyPoints: A function creates a local vector, builds a filter over it, and returns the filter.
The returned type may be perfectly well formed.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 18, treat Failure clinic — A returned pipeline that borrows a dead vector as a design decision with costs and evidence. A function creates a local vector, builds a filter over it, and returns the filter. The returned type may be perfectly well formed. The function still destroys its local vector on return, leaving the recipe without a valid source. Storing the returned view in a variable does not restore the destroyed elements. The appropriate repair is an owning result or a deliberately owning range arrangement whose dependencies are all valid. Another failure captures a local configuration object by reference inside a view that outlives the function. Even if the underlying vector lives long enough, the predicate’s configuration does not. Ownership analysis must include callable captures as well as the obvious element source. A diagram with only a view-to-vector arrow is incomplete when the predicate also points to local state. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 18, treat Guided lab — Choose an ownership boundary for report rows as a design decision with costs and evidence. Write a function that accepts a read-only collection of tasks and produces formatted rows for unfinished tasks. First return a view intended for immediate use by the caller, and document every borrowed dependency. Then write an owning-result version that can be retained after the input changes. Give the two functions names that communicate their different guarantees. Test empty input, no matches, all matches, and multiple priority groups. For the owning version, change or destroy the original input after the function returns and verify that the rows remain unchanged. For the borrowed version, keep all dependencies alive and unchanged throughout consumption; do not manufacture an invalid test merely to hope that a sanitizer catches it.
